By Clancy Balen

Topic:Mining and Metals Industry

Wed 10 Jun 2026 at 9:44am

Wed 10 Jun 2026 at 1:06pm

Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres made the announcement alongside Premier Jeremy Rockliff in Hobart on Wednesday. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The federal, Tasmanian and South Australian governments have announced $105 million in new funding to keep the Nyrstar smelters in Hobart and Port Pirie operating until the end of the year.

The money will also be used for feasibility studies into modernising and expanding both operations.

Nyrstar says the studies will help finalise the scope of major upgrades at the sites.

A further $105 million federal and state funding package has been announced for struggling Nyrstar smelters in Tasmania and South Australia.

Last August, Nyrstar received a $135 million joint funding package from the governments to keep the smelters in Hobart and Port Pirie in operation.

That funding — a $57.5 million contribution from the federal government, $55 million from South Australia, and $22.5 million from Tasmania — expired on May 1 this year.

The latest funding package helps secure the jobs of hundreds of workers at the Hobart smelter (pictured) and at Port Pirie.  (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

A joint federal and state announcement on Wednesday morning in Hobart said the new funding would support the continued operations of both smelters through to the end of 2026.

Tasmania contributed $7.5 million toward the new funding package, while South Australia contributed $35 million, and the Commonwealth put forward $62.5 million.

The fundng will help explore the possibility of producing antimony and other critical metals in Port Pirie. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

Speaking in Hobart on Wednesday morning, Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the funding would allow Nyrstar to complete a pre-feasibility study, and to progress work on a two-year feasibility study, to expand the production of critical and strategic minerals.

"This is not just an old facility with great capability; it is a facility that has got the capacity to punch forward into the future."

The bailout would secure about 550 direct jobs at the Hobart zinc smelter, and a further 1,000 indirect jobs across the state, Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff said.

About 800 people are employed directly at Nyrstar's Port Pirie smelter. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The Port Pirie smelter employs about 800 people directly.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said the possibility of producing antimony and other critical metals in Port Pirie presented a "unique opportunity".

"Antimony is a critical metal that is essential for defence applications, a suite of defence applications, and most of it at the moment is produced in China," he said at a press conference.

"Recently, China introduced an export ban on antimony to other parts of the world, which meant like-minded countries, like Australia and the US, were not able to get access to this critical defence material.

"By us being able to produce it in Port Pirie, it ensures that we have a sovereign capability in such a product."

Mr Malinauskas said the smelter not only mattered to the Port Pirie community, but the country as a whole.

"If we chose to do nothing, then I think it's almost certain that Nyrstar, in its current format, would no longer be operating in either Port Pirie or in Tasmania," Mr Malinauskas earlier told 891 ABC Adelaide.

The two smelters have been struggling to compete in the current global market.

In March last year, Nyrstar's parent company Trafigura said its smelters were "uncompetitive assets" and in June, revealed it was losing tens of millions of dollars per month over what it called a "distorted market".

Mr Ayres said the funding would be used to help re-industrialise the Australian economy.

"There's certainly challenges in the metals processing sector that are represented by market concentration and industrial subsidies, not just in China," Mr Ayres said.

"This is a facility that is capable of matching it in the global economy."

The general manager of the Hobart smelter, Todd Milne, said future funding may need to be sought in the future.

"We finish the pre-feasibility study in the next month or so and then the detailed feasibility work will continue through into the middle of next year," Mr Milne said.

Signage at Nyrstar zinc works, Hobart. (ABC News: David Robertson)

The funding, he said, would be used to supply base metals and critical metals to Australia's manufacturing supply chain.

"Things like sulphuric acid that we've produced here has been absolutely essential in Australia riding through some of the recent conflicts, like in the Strait of Hormuz," Mr Milne said.
